zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid (consulted after independent scan reading): NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Its headwords and derived kana do not establish this copy’s spelling or typography; the transcription follows the supplied BnF native scan.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Chamuſcar a Fune pera

lines.note: Continues tade from f463 with a transferred sense: singeing a boat. Fune is the Japanese boat-name embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: matar o bicho que a come.

lines.note: Completes the purpose of singeing: killing the wood-eating pest. The scan separately places “( Tade.” at the far right; its attachment is not silently reconstructed as ordinary running text.

runs.text: Hum Xiru frio feito deſta erua

lines.note: Tadebiyashiru is a cold soup made from the herb just discussed. Xiru is a Japanese food term embedded in the Portuguese gloss; the scan has no secure final period.
Tadori, tadoru, tadotta means feeling one’s way. The following literary example illustrates uncertain walking in darkness.

runs.text: Curaqi yoni ſocotomo xirazu touoqi mi-

lines.note: Kuraki yo ni soko tomo shirazu tōki michi… describes a dark night and a long road without knowing the location. Mi- begins michi across the physical line break.

Chi completes michi; tadorite ayumase tamayeba continues the honorific narrative about walking by feeling the way. The weak uo is retained from the visible object phrase, not replaced by the kana hint’s fragment.

runs.text: Andando eſte ſenhor como às apalpa-

lines.note: Feiq. is the upright literary citation label. The Portuguese begins its paraphrase of the lord walking as though feeling his way.

runs.text: delas em hũa noite eſcura ſem ſaber por onde

lines.note: Completes apalpadelas and describes a dark night in which he does not know where he is walking. The sentence closes on the next row.
Caminhaua closes the quotation’s translation. The separate far-right “( apalpadelas.” completes the following row’s “Modo de andar às”; its higher physical position is preserved.
Tadori tadori describes a groping manner of walking. The gloss’s final word is printed one row higher at the right, encoded under c1-l009 rather than moved here.
Tadori yuki means going here and there uncertainly. The principal form uita is printed; it is not recast as a modern inflection.

runs.text: pera là como às apalpadelas, ou como beba-

lines.note: Completes “here and there as if groping, or like a drunk person.” The scan shows a grave in às that the draft omitted; beba- continues below.
Do completes bebado, ending the comparison with unsteady drunken movement. This short continuation belongs to tadori yuki.

runs.text: Modo de ir às apalpadelas, ou

lines.note: Tadotadoxij describes going uncertainly, by feeling one’s way. The following row adds not knowing the road.
Completes “without knowing the road.” The final P. is the upright poetry-register label, not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Tadotadoxǔ is the adverbial form of the preceding adjective. The scan has a marked u, not OCR ǒ; Aduer. is italic grammatical apparatus.
Tafa is explained by uchiyaburu, destroying or breaking down. The Portuguese infinitives likewise denote destruction or undoing, with desfazer divided after desfa-.
The first word completes desfazer. The example warns against maintaining one’s own position while attacking another school or opinion; Iiriǔ and tafano are retained in the printed romanization.

runs.text: Deixai a condição de ſoſtentar voßa opinião,

lines.note: The Portuguese begins the injunction to abandon the habit of defending one’s own opinion. The opening is Deixai, not Deicai; its x is worn, and the whole translation is italic. The scan has opinião, including the internal i omitted by the draft.
This completes the injunction: stop demolishing the opinions of others. The ampersand and historical desfazer are preserved; the next headword belongs to the following physical row.
Tafit is another person’s handwriting, glossed by Betno fude. The scan reads Betno rather than the draft Betuo; the Portuguese is closely set as Letradoutra and is not modernized.

The alternative gloss is writing by another scribe. The r in eſcriuão survives only faintly and remains a nonblocking damaged-glyph reading; the draft’s internal space would not represent a separate word.
Tafǒ, with Bechino cata, means another side, direction or region. The marked final vowel and the partly abraded synonym are retained without replacing them by modern spellings.
The definition extends to another kingdom. This is an indented continuation of Tafǒ, not a separate entry.
Tafon is another copy or transcript, explained by Betno fon. The faint t of Betno is read by comparison with the same form in Tafit; treslado is the printed historical Portuguese spelling.
The headword is Tafu, not Taru: the worn f agrees with the coarse-cloth gloss Futoi nuno. The Portuguese says a thick cloth made from a tree bark; hũa ends this row without an added hyphen.

runs.text: caſca de aruore que ſerue de alimpar as mãos

lines.note: The cloth is made of tree bark and used to wipe the hands. Aruore and alimpar remain as printed; the text continues the material description from the preceding row.
The headword is Taga, not Tagu, with the alternative tarega. The dictionary gives both interrogative “who” and possessive “whose,” retaining the feminine cuia and the example marker Vt.
Taga coreuo itaitaca asks who did this. The Portuguese Quem fez isto? supplies the same question; the joining of the Japanese words is preserved as set.
Taga qiǒca asks whose book this is. The final vowel mark of qiǒ and the question mark are visible; the pilcrow introduces another example of the same headword.

Tagai is to differ or be at variance. Enlarged reinspection confirms a caron on the separate ǒ but no secure corresponding mark on ota, so the unaccented third form is retained as printed. Naca, l, begins an alternative construction continuing below.

Nacauo tagǒ is glossed as being estranged from another person in friendship. The phrase is incomplete at the physical line end and continues with amizade below; the final marked vowel of tagǒ is preserved.
Amizade completes the estrangement gloss. Fitono cocoroni tagǒ then describes going against someone’s feelings or wishes; the Portuguese translation starts at Dar and continues below.

runs.text: no coração dalguem, ou não lhe quadrar. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The explanation is to run counter to someone’s heart or not suit that person. The small stop after quadrar is retained; Itẽ is the printed nasal abbreviation introducing a further sense.

Te and Axi provide alternative examples about a hand or foot being displaced. The marked o in tagǒta is visible; the Portuguese has closely set Amão and opè, and the damaged predicate is read eſtã, not the draft eſã.
Fora de ſeu lugar completes the statement that the hand or foot is out of place. It belongs to the preceding examples, not to the following Tagaini entry.
Tagaini is labelled an adverb meaning mutually or among themselves. Entreſi is printed closely as one unit; Tagaini at the right begins the Japanese example continued below.
The example mǒxicauaſu concerns speaking to one another with a promise to do something. The marked o and the printed long-s form within the Japanese romanization are retained.
This completes the mutual-promise gloss: to do some thing. The nasal mark in algũa is visible, and the physical line is only the continuation of the preceding translation.

runs.text: Eſcopro com que cortão a prata.

lines.note: The headword begins with a capital T, not the draft’s r. Tagane is a chisel used to cut silver; Eſcopro, cortão and the final stop are preserved.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Buril com que abrem os ouriues.

lines.note: A second sense is a burin or graver used by goldsmiths for engraving. The mark after Item is a comma rather than a period; abrem is retained in its craft sense, not translated literally as opening a door.
Tagaraxi is described only as an herb of that name. No modern botanical identification is inserted, since this row itself gives none.
Tagaye gives the verb forms and begins a definition of differing from a person or failing to keep an undertaking. The initial Portuguese letter is D, not O; the t of tagayuru is worn but retained.

runs.text: ou não comprir a couſa prometida, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The alternative is failing to fulfil the promised thing. Historical comprir is kept rather than normalized to cumprir; Vt introduces the example on the next row.
Yacuſocuuo tagayuru means failing to keep a promise. The translation ends at pro- and must be completed by meßa on the following physical row.
Meßa completes promeßa. Dǒriuo tagayuru then denotes departing from reason; the initial vowel mark in Dǒriuo is retained and the Portuguese infinitive continues into the next row’s complement.
Da rezão completes the preceding gloss. Guiriuo tagayuru introduces conduct contrary to propriety; its Portuguese translation begins Não, not Nẽo, and runs directly into the top of column 2.

runs.text: ter primor, ou ir contra a boa policia, ou pri-

lines.note: This continues Não from the bottom of column 1: lacking propriety or acting against good manners. Policia has the older sense of civil conduct; pri- is completed by mor in the next row.

runs.text: mor. Ajuntaſe às raizes de algũs verbos, &

lines.note: Mor completes primor from the previous row. The entry then explains productive attachment to verb roots; the accented às and the nasal abbreviation algũs are retained.

runs.text: ſignifica fazer mal, ou errar a couſa que ſigni-

lines.note: When attached to a verb root, this element means doing the indicated act wrongly or mistaking its object. The second occurrence of ſignifica is physically broken after ſigni-.
Fica completes ſignifica. Mitagayuru is the first compound, meaning to see one thing as another; its translation begins Ver hũa and continues on the next row.
The first phrase completes the visual-mistake example. Qiqitagayuru then denotes mishearing: the enlarged scan has Qiqi-, not the draft’s Quiqi-. Portuguese Ou- continues as uir below.
The Portuguese completes “to hear one thing for another.” This is the continuation of the preceding compound example, with hũa carrying the visible nasal mark.
Tagaye is now entered as the act of erring or differing. Fito at the right begins an example about mistaking a person, not part of the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Não erreis a peßoa que buſ-

lines.note: Fito tagaye ſuna warns against getting the wrong person. Peßoa is fully present, correcting the truncated peſa in the draft; buſ- continues with cais on the next row.

runs.text: cais. i, Matando, ou fazendo mal a hum por

lines.note: Cais completes buſcais. The dictionary specifies the danger of killing or harming one person instead of another; the explanatory marker after cais is i followed by a comma.
Outro completes the mistaken-person explanation. Cadotagaye ſuru gives a mistaken door or house; the Portuguese starts Errar a, not the draft Eirara.
Porta, ou caſa completes the construction about getting the wrong door or house. It remains the indented continuation of the preceding example.

runs.text: Tornar o falcão à mão de quem

lines.note: Tagayeri describes a falcon returning to the hand of its former holder. The grave accent in à mão is visible, and the second Japanese form is the abbreviated u.
O tinha completes the identification of the person who had the falcon. No additional headword or sentence is present on this short continuation row.

Tagayexi is to cultivate or dig the fields. The crop includes the small final as beside the right rule; it is not the draft’s isolated n. Laurar is retained in its historical spelling rather than modernized.
Varzeas supplies the cultivated low-lying fields. The second letter is a rather than u; no modern accent is added to the visible unaccented spelling.
Taguen means many words, with Vouoi cotoba as its Japanese gloss. The Portuguese line ends with a semicolon, not a full stop, introducing the alternative description below.
The alternative is excessive speech. Muito corrects the draft muico; the proverb starts Taguenua miuo gai- and its last word continues on the following row.

runs.text: O muito falar mata a hum

lines.note: The initial ſu completes gaiſu. Xix. is an upright citation label, followed by the translation that much speaking kills a person; the label is kept separate from the italic Portuguese.
Homem completes the proverb’s translation. This short physical row has no further headword or text to supply.
Taguiǒ is explained by Yoſoye yuqu, going elsewhere or going out. The separation before yuqu is visible in the scan; the headword’s marked vowel and the example marker Vt at the right are retained.
These are two Japanese examples of going out, the latter in a polite form. There is no pilcrow before the first Taguiǒ in the scan, so the spurious draft marker has been removed.
Taguiri is the boiling of water. The row begins the marked figurative extension with ¶ Per, whose abbreviation continues as met. on the next physical row.
Cocorono taguiru applies boiling to the heart: being fervent. The italic met. completes the figurative label from above; cora- continues below as coração.
Ção completes coração, followed by the equivalent “to be fervent.” Taguitta fito is a Japanese noun phrase, introducing the description of a fervent person on the next row.
The translation is a fervent person. A further sense begins with Item, extending the image of boiling to the noise or agitation of flowing water.

runs.text: ſoar a agoa dalgum rio, ou da marè, que cor-

lines.note: The water may be that of a river or the tide, flowing vigorously. Marè retains the printed grave accent; cor- ends the row and continues with re on the next.
Re completes corre. The example describes a river running with surging force; the capital O at the right begins its Portuguese translation, rather than belonging to the Japanese example.

runs.text: rio com eſtrondo vai correndo, ou arrebatado.

lines.note: The river runs with a roaring noise or in a rushing torrent. The scan gives com eſtrondo and arrebatado, correcting the draft’s merged and misread words without modernizing vai or the historical expression.
Taguiricobore means to boil over. The faint r within the headword is retained, and the third form is eta, not ota; the Portuguese ends in fer-, continued below.
Uendo completes feruendo: the spilling occurs while boiling. The short row belongs wholly to the preceding verb definition.
Tago denotes buckets used to carry water. The example begins Ta- at the right and continues with gouo ninǒ on the next physical row.

runs.text: Leuar baldes dagoa de hũa par-

lines.note: This completes Tagouo ninǒ: carrying water buckets on both sides. The draft’s hnũia is a damaged reading of hũa; dagoa remains joined. The cramped mark after par at the right rule is retained as a hyphen, but its precise shape is worn; te continues the word below.

runs.text: te, & da outra a os ombros.

lines.note: Te completes parte. The buckets are carried on either side at the shoulders, consistent with a balanced carrying arrangement; the printed a os is left separate rather than normalized.
Tagǒ means another village or settlement, glossed by Betno mura. The scan supports Betno, not Bemno; the Portuguese po- continues as uoação below.
Uoação completes pouoação, the historical spelling of settlement. The cedilla and nasal mark remain as printed, with no new entry on this short continuation.
Tagon, glossed Tani cataru, is to speak or communicate to another person. Praticar is used in the older conversational sense, and cõmunicar carries the printed nasal abbreviation.
The definition specifies repeating to another what one has heard. Conocotouo at the right begins the example, which is completed in the next physical row.
Conocotouo tagon ſuruna tells someone not to speak about this to others. The Portuguese equivalent continues with peßoas below, while the joined ſuruna is preserved.
Peßoas completes the prohibition against telling other people. The final mark is retained as a stop; this is a continuation, not a new entry.

runs.text: Andas à maneira de cadeira ſem co-

lines.note: Tagoxi denotes a carrying chair or litter without a covering. The Portuguese compares it to a chair, and co- at the right continues with bertura below.
Bertura completes cobertura, followed by the further exclusion of a canopy or awning. The definition therefore specifies an uncovered carrying chair.
Taguri means gathering something by winding or coiling it. The Portuguese is Apanhar, not Apanbar; the abbreviated conjugated forms are retained in roman type.
Cords provide the concrete example of something gathered by coiling. Nauauo taguru is the standalone Japanese example; neither its words nor fragments are embedded-font candidates.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de nono, ou tea de linho.

lines.note: This separate Taguri entry names a kind of cloth or linen fabric. Nono is what is printed within the Portuguese explanation and is retained rather than silently normalized to the expected Japanese nuno; it is flagged as an embedded Japanese term.
Tagurui denotes disorderly or immodest play. Both abbreviated u forms carry the printed vowel mark; the Portuguese adverbial expression runs on to the next row.
Immodeſtamente completes the manner of playing. The double m and long s are historical printed forms and have not been modernized.

The final body row gives Taguye and its forms, labelling it a defective verb. The third form is taguyete, correcting the draft’s ç for g; the definition lies beyond this page and is previewed only by the separate catchword.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The catchword previews the beginning of the Taguye definition on the following page; it is not an additional body row.
